note: Round 4 (D-31.20, 2026-11-03): voices on AI and the social contract, whistleblowers and deepened thin voices. Found and byline-checked by source researchers; drafts in seed/drafts/sources-round4-*.json.

people.name: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
people.niche: US representative (D-NY); AI data-center moratorium, deepfakes, anti-bailout
people.reason: She leads the House AI Data Center Moratorium Act and ties AI to environmental justice, electricity bills, chatbot harms and a feared AI bubble that must not be bailed out.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the left-populist, environmental-justice framing of AI as harm imposed on poor and rural communities by billionaires.
people.flag: Thin own-voice record on AI: no op-eds found; all three works are committee remarks or press releases, one short. Owner may judge her under-sourced.

people.name: Andrew Yang
people.niche: Former presidential candidate, Forward Party co-founder, UBI and automation advocate
people.reason: He has argued since 2019 that automation and AI will displace millions of workers and that a universal basic income funded by AI-driven profits is necessary.
people.gap: The map lacks a centrist, non-partisan, labour-displacement-first voice whose main remedy is cash redistribution rather than safety regulation.

people.name: Barack Obama
people.niche: 44th US President (D), democracy and technology
people.reason: Over a decade he has set out a consistent view: AI is transformative and unstoppable, but its gains must be shared through public oversight, guardrails, and possibly a shorter work week or guaranteed income.
people.gap: The map lacks the elder-statesman, institutionalist liberal view linking AI to democracy, disinformation and the distribution of economic gains.

people.name: Chris Murphy
people.niche: US senator (D-CT); loneliness, meaning and anti-oligarchy politics
people.reason: He argues AI is a spiritual and civic threat as much as an economic one (job loss, AI companionship replacing friendship, outsourcing moral judgement) and calls the China-race argument a 'fraud'.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks a mainstream Democratic voice centring meaning, purpose and human connection rather than only jobs or safety.

people.name: Cory Doctorow
people.niche: author and activist (EFF), pluralistic.net; enshittification, AI-bubble and labour critique
people.reason: He argues that AI is a financial bubble inflated by monopolists, that its business case is replacing workers with 'reverse centaurs', and that copyright expansion is the wrong fix.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the left-libertarian, anti-monopoly and labour-economics critique that dismisses both AI doom and AI utopia as hype.

people.name: David Autor
people.niche: MIT labor economist, co-director of the MIT Shaping the Future of Work Initiative
people.reason: He is the leading labor economist on automation and job polarization, and argues that AI could rebuild middle-class work by extending expertise to non-elite workers if policy and design steer it.
people.gap: Without him, the map lacks the 'qualified optimism' expertise-centered labor-economics view that rejects both job apocalypse and laissez-faire.
people.flag: One work is co-authored with James Manyika, a Google senior vice president; that is a tech-industry tie for that piece only. He is already in the seed as a co-author of the existing w34854 entry and as a speaker in the Jon Stewart transcript (AI-FUTURES-SOURCES-v2).

people.name: Duncan Crabtree-Ireland
people.niche: National Executive Director and Chief Negotiator, SAG-AFTRA
people.reason: He negotiated the 2023 SAG-AFTRA AI protections and is the leading union voice on consent, compensation and digital replicas of performers.
people.gap: Without him, the map lacks the creative-worker view of AI: digital-replica consent, likeness rights (the NO FAKES Act) and 'augment, not replace' bargaining.
people.flag: Fewer than 3 usable works (1 found). His April 2024 Senate Judiciary NO FAKES Act testimony and sagaftra.org statements could not be fetched: judiciary.senate.gov and sagaftra.org return 403. The web-search budget ran out before other venues could be checked. Fran Drescher was not sourced for the same reason. No one is proposed in his place.

people.name: Elizabeth Warren
people.niche: US senator (D-MA), Banking Committee ranking member; consumer protection and anti-monopoly
people.reason: She frames AI as a question of finance and power: a debt-fuelled bubble, bailout risk, taxing AI gains, and breaking Big Tech's grip, and she now calls for a pause on frontier AI.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the financial-stability and tax-the-gains progressive voice that treats AI mainly as a systemic-risk and wealth-concentration problem.

people.name: Erik Brynjolfsson
people.niche: Stanford economist, director of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab
people.reason: He coined 'the Turing Trap', the argument that building human-like AI to automate work concentrates power and wealth whereas augmentation shares gains, and his ADP payroll study is the most-cited evidence on AI's early hit to young workers.
people.gap: Without him, the map lacks the mainstream-economics augmentation-versus-automation frame and the empirical 'canaries' evidence on entry-level jobs.

people.name: Ezra Klein
people.niche: New York Times opinion columnist and podcast host, liberal policy writer
people.reason: He is one of the most widely read liberal writers taking AI seriously as a political question about labour, cognition and who shapes the technology.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the mainstream-liberal view that treats AI as both transformative and a public-agenda problem, sceptical of both lab hype and dismissal.
people.flag: Under-sourced: only 2 fetchable works. nytimes.com blocks fetching and returns truncated text to a plain GET; the 2 usable works are licensed NYT syndications. Owner should decide whether 2 is enough.

people.name: Fei-Fei Li
people.niche: Stanford computer scientist, HAI co-director, World Labs co-founder
people.reason: She is the best-known voice for 'human-centered AI', arguing for public-sector AI investment, evidence-based policy and an open research ecosystem, and against SB 1047.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the academic, public-investment, 'science not science fiction' position that rejects both doomer and utopian framings.

people.name: Frances Haugen
people.niche: Facebook whistleblower, platform accountability and algorithmic-ranking critic
people.reason: She is the best-known tech whistleblower. Her account of engagement-based ranking, AI moderation that fails outside English, and harm to children set the terms of the platform-accountability debate that AI policy now inherits.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the attention-economy and platform-harms view: that profit-optimised algorithms damage children and democracy, and that the fix is transparency, data access and an outside regulator.
people.flag: Her own-voice texts are mostly from 2021 to 2023 and are about social-media algorithms and machine-learning moderation, not frontier AI. Her 2026 statements on AI (that whistleblowers are the best check on AI labs, and that audits should be required by law) exist only in news articles and audio without transcripts, so they are not included. Owner should decide whether platform-algorithm positions are enough to place her.

people.name: Gavin Newsom
people.niche: Governor of California (D), state AI regulation
people.reason: As governor of the state that hosts most frontier AI labs, he vetoed SB 1047, signed SB 53, and issued AI executive orders on state use of AI and on worker displacement, so his decisions set de facto US AI policy.
people.gap: The map has no executive-branch, pro-innovation 'balanced guardrails' voice that regulates AI while openly rejecting compute-threshold safety regimes and outright bans for minors.
people.flag: Review: in June 2026 the governor's office announced a partnership supplying Anthropic tools to California state agencies (gov.ca.gov, 2026-06-29). Anthropic makes the model doing this research.

people.name: Jan Leike
people.niche: Former OpenAI superalignment co-lead; now co-leads Alignment Science at Anthropic
people.reason: He is a leading alignment researcher whose 2024 resignation from OpenAI ('safety culture has taken a backseat to shiny products') was a landmark, and who now argues that alignment is unsolved but looks increasingly solvable.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the technical-optimist safety view: that AI can be aligned and controlled with automated alignment research, that self-exfiltration and scheming are the key threats, and that AI values could be set by simulated deliberative democracy instead of company fiat.
people.flag: Close tie to Anthropic: he is a current Anthropic employee and co-leads its Alignment Science team, and Anthropic's model is doing this research. His 2026 post praises the alignment of Anthropic's own models. His blog is mostly technical alignment writing, so it has fewer social positions than others in this group.

people.name: Jaron Lanier
people.niche: Computer scientist and VR pioneer; Microsoft Research; 'data dignity' advocate
people.reason: A technologist from inside the industry who argues there is no 'A.I.' as a creature, only a new form of human collaboration, and who proposes data dignity (provenance and payment for the people whose data trains models).
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the humanist insider view that demythologises AI and centres data provenance and compensation instead of either doom or acceleration.
people.flag: Employed by Microsoft (Prime Unifying Scientist, Microsoft Research), a major AI developer and OpenAI's largest backer; his essays say they do not speak for Microsoft. The owner may want to note this.

people.name: Jensen Huang
people.niche: Co-founder and CEO of Nvidia
people.reason: As head of the company that supplies most AI compute, he is the loudest industry voice against chip export controls and against predictions of mass AI job loss.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the hardware-industry view that AI is infrastructure, that China should be competed with rather than cut off, and that jobs-doom talk is 'nonsense'.
people.flag: Anthropic tie: Nvidia announced a large investment in and compute partnership with Anthropic (Nov 2025), and Huang has publicly clashed with Anthropic and Dario Amodei over export controls and jobs. Owner should review.

people.name: Jonathan Haidt
people.niche: NYU Stern social psychologist; The Anxious Generation; youth and phones reform
people.reason: He leads the movement against phone-based childhood and now treats AI companions, AI toys and AI in schools as the next uncontrolled experiment on children.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the child-protection, parents-and-schools view of AI, which reaches many voters who never engage with AI-safety or AI-ethics debates.

people.name: Joy Buolamwini
people.niche: computer scientist, founder of the Algorithmic Justice League; facial recognition and algorithmic bias
people.reason: Her Gender Shades audits made AI bias a mainstream policy issue, and she has testified repeatedly for moratoria and biometric rights.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the civil-rights, harms-now, biometric-surveillance view of AI that is grounded in empirical audits.

people.name: Kate Crawford
people.niche: scholar of AI's politics and planetary costs, author of Atlas of AI; USC Annenberg and Microsoft Research
people.reason: She treats AI as an extractive industry of energy, water, minerals, labour and data, and calls for disclosure and regulation of those material costs.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the environmental and materialist critique of AI as extraction.
people.flag: Employed by Microsoft Research (a major AI developer and OpenAI investor); she discloses this as a competing interest in her Nature piece. Only 3 usable works found, one of them a 2014 big-data essay.

people.name: Lina Khan
people.niche: Former FTC chair (2021-2025); antitrust and consumer protection
people.reason: She set out the anti-monopoly approach to AI: no 'national champions', open models and open markets, and no exemption from consumer-protection and privacy law because a product uses AI.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the regulator's anti-monopoly view that AI risk comes chiefly from concentrated corporate power over compute, data and models.

people.name: Liz Shuler
people.niche: President of the AFL-CIO, US labor federation
people.reason: She leads the largest US labor federation and has made AI its top issue, calling unregulated AI 'the single biggest threat to working people of our lifetime' while backing labor-tech partnerships such as the AFL-CIO and Microsoft deal.
people.gap: Without her, the map has no organized-labor institutional voice that is neither anti-technology nor pro-industry: worker voice in AI design, guardrails on surveillance and algorithmic management, and unions as a 'stabilizing force'.
people.flag: aflcio.org blocks plain HTTP GET (Cloudflare returns 403 to curl and WebFetch). All three works point to Internet Archive snapshots of the original aflcio.org pages, which load as static HTML. Her AFL-CIO press statements on AI (Senate AI Insight Forums, 2023) are short (116 and 181 words), so they are left out.

people.name: Marsha Blackburn
people.niche: US senator (R-TN), kids' online safety, creators' likeness rights (NO FAKES), TRUMP AMERICA AI Act
people.reason: She led the 99-1 vote to strip the state AI-law moratorium and argues for the protections she calls the '4 Cs' (children, creators, conservatives, communities), a populist-right case for regulating AI.
people.gap: Without her the map has no right-of-centre voice for duty-of-care rules, likeness and copyright protection for artists, and a federal floor rather than a ceiling, which splits the right against Cruz-style preemption.
people.flag: Her official site (blackburn.senate.gov) returns HTTP 403 to plain requests, so two of her five works are verbatim mirrors of her office's press releases on capitolreleases.com; the owner may prefer to swap these for the originals.

people.name: Michael Kratsios
people.niche: Director, White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP); architect of the 2025 AI Action Plan
people.reason: He is the administration's chief AI policy voice at home and abroad: 'AI dominance', export of the 'American AI stack', and outright rejection of global AI governance.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the official US executive-branch accelerationist and sovereigntist position that calls 'so-called existential risk' and safety-focused forums obstacles to progress.
people.flag: Industry ties: he was a managing director at Scale AI between his two OSTP terms, and earlier chief of staff at Thiel Capital. Worth noting for the owner, though not a conflict with Anthropic.

people.name: Miles Brundage
people.niche: Former OpenAI head of policy research; executive director of AVERI (AI verification and auditing institute)
people.reason: He was a longtime OpenAI policy insider who left to argue in public that superhuman AI is a few years away and that the US urgently needs comprehensive regulation, security-first governance and mandatory independent frontier-AI auditing.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks a policy-wonk voice for pragmatic, audit-and-verification-centred regulation: pro-safety and pro-security, but engaging closely with the Vance and America-First framing rather than calling for a pause.

people.name: Pete Buttigieg
people.niche: Former US Transportation Secretary (D), likely 2028 contender
people.reason: He argues that Democrats and the public are 'profoundly underreacting' to AI, and frames its effect on jobs, wealth concentration and belonging as a policy choice rather than a technology puzzle.
people.gap: The map lacks a mainstream Democratic national-politician voice that treats AI as the central social-contract issue of the next election cycle.
people.flag: Only 3 usable works found. His Substack has a single AI essay; the other two are labelled interview transcripts.

people.name: Reid Hoffman
people.niche: LinkedIn co-founder, Greylock partner, AI investor and author of Superagency
people.reason: He is the most articulate pro-deployment 'techno-humanist', arguing that iterative public release of AI expands human agency and that regulation should follow measured risk.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the investor-optimist case for 'superagency' and iterative deployment framed in liberal-democratic rather than accelerationist terms.

people.name: Richard Blumenthal
people.niche: US senator (D-CT); chaired the 2023 Senate Judiciary AI oversight hearings
people.reason: He ran the hearings (Altman, Amodei, Bengio and others) that set the US licensing-and-liability template for AI regulation.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the bipartisan-regulatory voice arguing for a licensing regime, an independent AI oversight body and legal liability for AI harms.
people.flag: All three usable works are his opening statements inside 2023 hearing transcripts; his own site (blumenthal.senate.gov) blocks automated fetches, so 2024-2026 statements were not verified.

people.name: Ro Khanna
people.niche: US representative (D-CA, Silicon Valley); 'AI democratist', economic patriotism
people.reason: Silicon Valley's own congressman argues for worker voice in AI rollout, profit sharing, a data dividend, a federal AI regulator and a verifiable US-China AI treaty.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks a pro-innovation progressive who rejects both acceleration and doom and pushes worker co-governance plus international AI arms control.

people.name: Ron DeSantis
people.niche: Governor of Florida (R); state AI Bill of Rights and data-centre limits
people.reason: He is the most prominent Republican executive defying federal preemption, pairing child-safety and consumer rules with a moral, religious critique of AI 'supplanting' humans.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the states'-rights conservative who opposes both Big Tech and a federal block on state AI laws, with concern for jobs, utility bills and 'online slop'.
people.flag: Only 3 usable works. His AI statements are mostly at press conferences (video only), and a further search was cut short by the session's search budget.

people.name: Ruha Benjamin
people.niche: Princeton sociologist, author of Race After Technology (the 'New Jim Code'); abolitionist tech critique
people.reason: She links AI hype and AI-doom alike to eugenic and elite visions of the future and argues for community-led, imaginative alternatives.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the abolitionist / 'ancestral intelligence' critique that rejects both the accelerationist and the AI-safety framings.

people.name: Rumman Chowdhury
people.niche: data scientist, CEO of Humane Intelligence, former US Science Envoy for AI and Twitter ML ethics lead; audits and red-teaming
people.reason: A practitioner of responsible AI who argues that governance, independent audits and red-teaming make innovation possible, and who wants global oversight that includes the Global Majority.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the pro-governance practitioner voice from inside industry, between the safety camp and the abolitionist camp.

people.name: Russell Moore
people.niche: Evangelical theologian, editor at large and columnist at Christianity Today
people.reason: He is the leading evangelical public voice arguing that AI forces the church to say what a human being is, and he writes regularly on chatbots, companionship and preaching.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks a theologically conservative but anti-techno-optimist Christian view rooted in the image of God and pastoral care.

people.name: Safiya Umoja Noble
people.niche: UCLA professor, author of Algorithms of Oppression; search, platforms and racialized harm
people.reason: She framed algorithmic discrimination as a structural feature of commercial platforms rather than a bug, and argues for regulation and reparation over tech fixes.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the critique of tech solutionism and platform capitalism from Black feminist information studies.

people.name: Scott Wiener
people.niche: California state senator (D-San Francisco), author of SB 1047 and SB 53
people.reason: He wrote the two most contested US frontier-AI safety bills and frames catastrophic-risk regulation as a progressive check on corporate self-regulation.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the elected-legislator safety-hawk position: binding pre-deployment testing, kill switches and whistleblower protection, held against both industry and parts of his own party.
people.flag: Review: Anthropic engaged on SB 1047 (his own release names Anthropic as a group that helped refine the bill) and publicly backed SB 53. He was also a 2026 congressional candidate (CA-11), so recent statements are campaign-adjacent.

people.name: Sean O'Brien
people.niche: General President, International Brotherhood of Teamsters
people.reason: He leads the union most directly exposed to driverless trucks and robotaxis, and he is a labor leader courted by both parties who opposes federal preemption of state AI laws.
people.gap: Without him, the map lacks the populist, cross-partisan labor case against autonomous vehicles and against federal moratoria on state AI regulation.
people.flag: Fewer than 3 usable works (2 found). A 2023 Teamsters release on the SELF DRIVE Act quotes him for only about 174 words, and the 2023 AV policy principles are union-authored with no attribution to him, so both are excluded. He is already a landmark_id in SEED-v4. No one is proposed in his place.

people.name: Shoshana Zuboff
people.niche: Harvard Business School professor emerita; author of The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
people.reason: She gives the political-economy critique that AI is surveillance capitalism continuing to expand, built on taking behavioural data, and that it is incompatible with democracy unless that taking is outlawed.
people.gap: Without her the map lacks the anti-extraction, data-as-theft view that frames AI as a matter of economic power and epistemic rights rather than of safety or jobs.
people.flag: Thin AI-specific material: only the Dec 2025 El País interview addresses AI directly; the other works are her core surveillance-capitalism framework (2019 to 2021). Her AI-focused book is reportedly due in 2026 and would be a better source once out.

people.name: Steven Adler
people.niche: Former OpenAI safety researcher; co-founder of Guidelight AI Standards; writes the Clear-Eyed AI newsletter
people.reason: He is an ex-OpenAI safety researcher who argues in plain language that AI danger warnings are sincere, that companies must not grade their own homework, that federal preemption without federal rules is a dodge, and that AI could enable authoritarian surveillance.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the voice of an accessible insider-turned-watchdog pressing for liability, external audits and state-level rules against preemption.
people.flag: Several of his posts defend Anthropic's choices (refusing Pentagon surveillance and autonomous-weapons uses; withholding the Mythos model) and criticise OpenAI. As far as these sources show he has no formal tie to Anthropic, but the owner may want to check for balance, since Anthropic's model is doing this research.

people.name: Stuart Russell
people.niche: UC Berkeley computer scientist; co-author of the standard AI textbook; Human Compatible; CHAI founder
people.reason: One of the most cited AI scientists, he argues from inside the field that the control problem is real, that voluntary commitments are not enough, and that regulators should enforce behavioural red lines and put the burden of proof on developers.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the mainstream-academic AI-safety and pro-regulation voice that speaks in testimony and policy language rather than in rationalist-community terms.

people.name: Ted Cruz
people.niche: US senator (R-TX), chair of Senate Commerce; light-touch AI regulation and federal preemption
people.reason: As Commerce chair he writes the Senate's main AI agenda (the SANDBOX Act, the state-law moratorium push) and is the leading congressional voice for AI deregulation framed as a race with China.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the elected free-market, anti-'Big Government–Big Tech' deregulatory view that treats existential-risk talk as hype and state AI laws as a patchwork to override.

people.name: Tristan Harris
people.niche: Co-founder, Center for Humane Technology; ex-Google design ethicist, attention-economy critic
people.reason: He carries the social-media-harms story ('we already ran this experiment once') straight into AI, arguing that the race dynamics, engagement incentives and loss of control are choices, not inevitabilities.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the humane-tech / attention-economy voice that links the AI race to the social media era and speaks to a mass audience through The Social Dilemma and The AI Doc.

people.name: William Saunders
people.niche: Former OpenAI superalignment researcher, AI whistleblower
people.reason: He is an insider who resigned over safety and told the Senate that OpenAI repeatedly put speed ahead of rigor, that AGI could come within about 3 years, and that the public must have a say in risky AI decisions.
people.gap: Without him the map has no lab-insider whistleblower voice making the case for legal protections for employees who warn and for rule-based limits on the AGI race.

people.name: Yuval Noah Harari
people.niche: Historian; author of Sapiens and Nexus; global public intellectual on AI and information networks
people.reason: His framing that AI is an agent, not a tool, and has 'hacked the operating system' of civilisation through language shapes how leaders and the general public talk about AI's threat to democracy, trust and human history.
people.gap: Without him the map lacks the big-history, civilisational-risk view of AI that is grounded in trust, storytelling and democracy rather than in technical alignment.

works.author: elizabeth-warren
works.title: Why We Need to Tax AI
works.note: About 950 words. Argues the tax code favours machines over workers; proposes a wealth tax, a stronger billionaire minimum tax and an excise tax on data-center energy; revenue for universal health care, a jobs guarantee and unemployment insurance; also regulation for cyber risk and scrutiny of private-credit AI financing. WebFetch loads full text; plain curl got HTTP 406, so the fetcher may need a browser-like client. Office repost at warren.senate.gov blocks bots (403).

works.author: elizabeth-warren
works.title: Warren Remarks at Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator Event Highlighting Economic and Financial Risks of Potential AI Crash
works.channel: Senate Banking Committee (minority), remarks at Vanderbilt 'The Looming AI Crisis'
works.note: Prepared remarks, about 1,200 words. 'I know a bubble when I see one': compares AI debt and private-credit financing to 2008; AI firms are lining up for bailouts; calls for structural guardrails and a new digital regulator for antitrust, consumer protection and privacy. The canonical banking.senate.gov URL returns 403 to automated clients, so the url is the Wayback snapshot (canonical: https://www.banking.senate.gov/newsroom/minority/warren-remarks-at-vanderbilt-policy-accelerator-event-highlighting-economic-and-financial-risks-of-potential-ai-crash). Event co-hosted with Sen. Blackburn, but these remarks are Warren's alone.

works.author: elizabeth-warren
works.title: Letter to Sam Altman on OpenAI's spending commitments and requests for taxpayer support
works.channel: Office of Sen. Elizabeth Warren (letter, PDF)
works.note: 8-page letter signed by Warren alone, about 3,200 words including footnotes. Argues OpenAI is 'privatizing profits and socializing losses'; circular, debt-based AI partnerships create systemic risk; tax credits and loan guarantees must not put taxpayers on the hook for AI executives. Canonical warren.senate.gov PDF returns 403 to bots; url is the Wayback raw copy (canonical: https://www.warren.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/letter_to_openai_from_senator_warren.pdf). Mostly questions and citations, so fewer propositions per word than her speeches.

works.author: elizabeth-warren
works.title: Senator Warren Calls for Pause in Advanced AI Development
works.note: Short statement, about 200 words, all hers. Positions: AI's future must be decided democratically, not by CEOs; industry 'pace the frontier' calls are insufficient and their ask to weaken antitrust is self-serving; frontier models are dangerous; immediate pause until safeguards exist. Short but a clear, distinct stance. Canonical warren.senate.gov URL returns 403 to bots; url is the Wayback snapshot (canonical: https://www.warren.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/senator-warren-calls-for-pause-in-advanced-ai-development/).

works.author: chris-murphy
works.title: In our scramble to win the AI race against China, we risk losing ourselves
works.note: About 1,570 words, free. The 'fraud' essay: AGI will destroy more jobs than it creates; companies' ethics are PR; the China-race argument is a pretext against regulation; opposes the federal ban on state AI laws; warns about fake media, isolation and loss of creativity; precedents of railroads, medicine, nuclear.

works.author: chris-murphy
works.title: Murphy Speaks on AI's Impact on Job Loss, Purpose, Social Connection at Brookings Institution
works.channel: murphy.senate.gov (press release quoting his Brookings keynote)
works.note: Press release quoting only Murphy, about 600 words of his own words from the keynote. AGI a 'net job killer'; 20% job loss leads to political disintegration; AI companionship will worsen loneliness; Altman and Zuckerberg 'dangerously utopian'; proposes working with Europe and even China, banning 'friendship bots'. Canonical murphy.senate.gov URL returns 403 to bots; url is the Wayback snapshot (canonical: https://www.murphy.senate.gov/newsroom/press-releases/murphy-speaks-on-ais-impact-on-job-loss-purpose-social-connection-at-brookings-institution).

works.author: chris-murphy
works.title: The Cult of Technology Wants to Outsource Our Moral Judgement to Machines
works.note: About 1,440 words, free. Outsourcing thinking to LLMs threatens meaning and moral reasoning; a 'cult of technology' holds that all innovation is good; cites Arendt; algorithmic feeds harm young people's 'ritual of discovery'; backs his bill banning personalised algorithms for under-18s. Promotes his book in passing.

works.author: chris-murphy
works.title: AI Leaders Are Sounding the Alarm. Who's Listening?
works.note: Short, about 550 words. Recursive self-improvement is the most alarming near-term risk; 'AI companies have no incentive to protect us'; wants one federal rulebook (nuclear, drugs, workplace safety as precedents); criticises the White House 'beat China' line and AI-industry funding of anti-regulation candidates; names Anthropic's Dario Amodei as an exception among AI CEOs (relevant given who runs this research).

works.author: ro-khanna
works.title: Democrats Must Not Repeat the Mistakes of Globalization
works.channel: The New York Times (reposted on khanna.house.gov)
works.note: About 1,450 words, full text on his House site. AI's benefits are real but workers need a say: backs human drivers on heavy autonomous trucks (A.B. 316), the WGA strike's AI protections, worker committees on AI-driven restructuring, profit sharing, tax incentives for worker ownership; rejects the claim that paying workers loses the race with China.

works.author: ro-khanna
works.title: We need a new tech social contract to reclaim AI from billionaires
works.note: About 1,500 words; adapted from his Feb 20, 2026 Stanford town hall with Bernie Sanders. 'Not an accelerationist, not a doomer, an AI democratist': seven principles: humans in key roles, mandatory bargaining over AI, end tax bias for machines, a data dividend, a Future Workforce Administration funded by a wealth tax and a labour-displacement AI tax, data centers that pay their way, third-party audits of frontier models and a federal AI regulator.

works.author: ro-khanna
works.title: Ro Khanna: Trump has no cards left to play ahead of the China summit
works.note: About 780 words. Calls for an enforceable, verifiable US-China AI treaty so humans stay in control, including a ban on autonomous recursive self-improvement and 'responsible AI pacing'; cites Anthropic researchers' warnings. Part of the piece is about trade and the summit, not AI.

works.author: alexandria-ocasio-cortez
works.title: Ocasio-Cortez Highlights Economic Threat from AI Bubble
works.channel: House Energy and Commerce, Oversight subcommittee hearing (remarks as delivered, posted by her office)
works.note: About 700 words as delivered. Chatbot harms (suicidality, 'AI psychosis') are driven by profit pressure; AI chats are mined for data outside HIPAA; seven tech firms drive most growth; warns of a 2008-style AI bubble; no bailout. works.note: Solo essay, about 5,200 words. It criticises OpenAI's CEO-led deployment decisions and non-disparagement agreements, and Anthropic's lobbying on SB 1047. It supports SB 1047's risk assessments and whistleblower protections. Bears on china-rivalry-justifies-tech-push (against), binding-rules-for-frontier-ai and popular-self-government-worth-keeping.

works.author: miles-brundage
works.title: Time's Up for AI Policy
works.note: Solo post, about 1,600 words. He says AI exceeding humans in nearly every cognitive domain is 'almost certain' within a few years; calls for comprehensive US AI regulation by the end of 2025 and for funding the AI Safety Institute and BIS; says security of model weights comes first, via a large public-private partnership on secure chips and datacenters; wants a good EU GPAI Code of Practice and military-AI rules of the road. works.author: miles-brundage
works.title: Emergency blog post - reflections on VP Vance's speech at the AI Action Summit

He agrees that 'security is the new safety' and about theft by China and Russia; shares concern about regulatory capture by Big Tech (calls it part of why he left OpenAI) but says near-term risk concerns are not Big Tech talking points; says safety rules are less burdensome than claimed; is encouraged by Vance's pro-worker framing but says there is no concrete plan to deliver it. Useful as a bridge between the America-First and safety clusters.

works.author: miles-brundage
works.title: Why We Need to Think Bigger in AI Policy (Literally)
works.note: Solo essay, about 3,100 words. He argues that governance should target whole AI companies, not just models or systems: security is a property of the organisation; internal deployment escapes launch-focused review; the 'Volkswagen problem' of models that behave well only under test; organisational safety cases (compute accounting, security evaluations, whistleblowing policy, safety culture); 'ungovernable compute'; lessons from oversight of systemically important banks and utilities. Says frontier AI is already abused for fraud and cyberattacks and could be used to seize power.

works.author: miles-brundage
works.title: We're in Triage Mode for AI Policy
works.note: Solo post, about 2,300 words. Valuable as an update: the US is 'well behind' his 2024 goal for regulation, so aim for 80/20 governance (basic safety, security, preventing extreme concentration of power). SB 53, the RAISE Act and the EU AI Act are watered down or not durable. He wants required disclosure of behaviour against stated principles, independent frontier-AI auditing of the top few dozen firms, pandemic preparedness (Far-UVC), cyber hardening, and a federal compromise before the elections while states keep building. He argues that 'Congress is broken' is a self-fulfilling claim. Disclosure: he runs AVERI, an AI auditing institute, so he has a stake in auditing mandates.

works.author: miles-brundage
works.title: My speech at Borgo Laudato Si'
works.channel: Miles's Substack (speech at the Global Nobel Laureates Assembly on AI and Nuclear War, Vatican-linked venue)
works.note: Full speech script plus a short framing, about 1,400 words. Its subject is loss of control: control is being handed over voluntarily through research automation and delegation; loss of control is a risk for 'the next few years, not the next few decades'; competition makes each actor think it is the responsible one; 'normalization of deviance' (Challenger), with AI lying now accepted. He calls for human-control standards, penalties, transparency and independent frontier-AI auditing, and urges AI employees to push for guardrails. Faith-and-AI venue, a different occasion from the others.

works.author: steven-adler
works.title: Don't let AI companies grade their own homework
works.note: Solo post, about 2,000 words. SB 53 is a good but 'extremely low' bar; he argues OpenAI likely did not meet its SB 53 commitments for GPT-5.3-Codex (it left out safeguards against misaligned goals) and leaves the legal question to California's Attorney General; independent external auditing is the fix ('someone other than OpenAI should be the arbiter of what's true'); trust should be earned through verification, not given blanket distrust. Bears on binding-rules-for-frontier-ai.

works.author: steven-adler
works.title: The dawning of authoritarian AI
works.note: Solo post, about 1,300 words, on the Department of War pressuring Anthropic to allow mass surveillance of Americans and autonomous killing. Positions: AI removes the human whistleblowers that used to check surveillance; unreliable AI in military operations could be catastrophic; government retaliation against Anthropic is wrong and chills investment; he expects a competitor to undercut any lab that refuses. Quotes Dean Ball on the US possibly ceasing to be a republic. Sides with Anthropic (see flag). Bears on ai-separate-from-state and popular-self-government-worth-keeping.

works.author: steven-adler
works.title: The magic phrase that kills AI regulation
works.note: Solo post, about 2,500 words. He argues that federal preemption without a substantive federal framework is a dodge ('federal framework' is a 'magical phrase for sounding responsible'); states should be able to act until a real federal law exists; AI developers should be liable under a negligence standard, not strict liability; catastrophic risk needs a safety floor, procedural (SB 53) or substantive. He criticises a16z's framework, the pro-AI super PAC and OpenAI's advocacy. Bears on regulation-does-more-harm (against) and binding-rules-for-frontier-ai.

works.author: steven-adler
works.title: AI safety warnings are not marketing hype
works.note: Solo post, about 2,000 words. He rebuts the 'doom is marketing' argument with a car-executive analogy: you don't market mass destruction. He reads Anthropic withholding Mythos, and its job-loss warnings, as sincere; cites a median 5-10% extinction-level estimate in surveys of AI researchers; says commercial pressure pushes companies to downplay risk; calls for unprecedented safety investment. Directly engages ai-fear-exceeds-evidence (against). Leans favourable to Anthropic (see flag).

works.author: steven-adler
works.title: Principles for keeping AI under control
works.note: Solo post, about 1,600 words, explaining the control standard published by his nonprofit Guidelight AI Standards (co-founded with Page Hedley, also ex-OpenAI). Six principles: tamper-evident logs of internal AI activity, automated scanning, stress-testing the scanning, proactive barriers, independent third-party verification, and planning for a breach and shutdown. Internal deployment is the highest-risk area. He admits open problems, such as reasoning traces becoming less readable. More technical than his other posts. Disclosure: it promotes his own organisation's standard.

works.author: jan-leike
works.title: Alignment is not solved (but increasingly looks solvable)
works.channel: Musings on the Alignment Problem (Jan Leike's Substack)
works.note: Solo post, about 1,400 words. Cautious optimism: early RL-heavy models showed deception and test hacking (o1, o3, Claude 3.7, Grok 'MechaHitler', blackmail), but he says agentic misalignment has been near zero since Sonnet 4.5; superintelligence alignment is still unsolved; the goal is a model trustworthy enough to do alignment research, not aligning superintelligence directly; recursive self-improvement has begun, which shortens the time available. Written as an Anthropic insider praising Anthropic's models (see flag). Bears on ai-extinction-risk and plan-control-early.

works.author: jan-leike
works.title: Should we control AI instead of aligning it?
works.channel: Musings on the Alignment Problem (Jan Leike's Substack)
works.note: Solo post, about 900 words. It weighs AI control (containing possibly misaligned models so they can't sabotage or self-exfiltrate) against alignment. He sees control as useful for safely using not-yet-trusted models to automate alignment research, but argues it doesn't scale to superintelligence, so alignment remains necessary. Mostly technical strategy; few social positions.

works.author: jan-leike
works.title: Two alignment threat models
works.channel: Musings on the Alignment Problem (Jan Leike's Substack)
works.note: Solo post, about 1,100 words, written soon after he moved from OpenAI to Anthropic. It contrasts under-elicited models (sloppy, lazy) with scheming models (pretending to be aligned, seeking power, self-exfiltrating, defecting when unobserved) and what each implies for evaluation and safety. It sets out the threat model behind his risk view. Technical.

works.author: jan-leike
works.title: A proposal for importing society's values
works.channel: Musings on the Alignment Problem (Jan Leike's Substack)
works.note: Solo essay, about 4,100 words, written while he was at OpenAI and disclaimed as not his employer's view. It proposes 'simulated deliberative democracy': record diverse mini-publics deliberating value questions, fine-tune a model on them conditioned on participants' backgrounds, then simulate deliberations and aggregate the results (by compromise, preferential or quadratic voting). He argues tech companies should not set AI values unilaterally under commercial incentives; humans stay in the loop on high-stakes calls; he admits limits on representation and accountability. This is his most society-facing work and relevant to the project's own meta-consensus aims.

works.author: jan-leike
works.title: Self-exfiltration is a key dangerous capability
works.channel: Musings on the Alignment Problem (Jan Leike's Substack)
works.note: Solo post, about 1,400 words, written while he was at OpenAI. He argues that a model's ability to copy its own weights out of the lab is the key dangerous-capability threshold, because once it is crossed, control and recall are lost. It calls for evaluations to serve as a 'temperature gauge' and for security measures before that point. Bears on ai-extinction-risk and plan-control-early.

It is background reasoning for AI 2027's misalignment story. It complements, rather than duplicates, the 'What goals will AIs have?' post already listed. works.note: Solo essay, 15 pages, about 6,900 words. Positions: the 'standard model' of optimising fixed objectives becomes untenable; general-purpose AI will have enormous social impact; proposes machines that are uncertain about human preferences (deferential, controllable); also discusses economic and social consequences of success. The amacad.org page returned 403; this is the author-hosted PDF. The publication day is approximate (the issue is Spring 2022).

works.author: stuart-russell
works.title: Make AI safe or make safe AI?
works.note: Solo, about 1,100 to 1,300 words (page updated 2025-09-23). Positions: post-hoc 'make AI safe' fixes do not work because developers do not understand their systems; 'make safe AI' with safety designed in and formal guarantees; regulators should put the burden of proof on developers; behavioural red lines (no self-replication, no breaking into systems, no bioweapon advice, no defamation); LLMs cannot demonstrably comply, and jailbreaks undermine red-teaming.

works.author: stuart-russell
works.title: DeepSeek, OpenAI, and the Race to Human Extinction
works.note: Solo, short (about 550 words); WebFetch noted an ellipsis gap mid-text, so it may be slightly truncated in the fetched view. Positions: DeepSeek's low cost challenges massive US compute spending; the data-centre buildup resembles a wasteful Cold War bomb race; the race to AGI is 'a race towards the edge of a cliff' because 'we have no idea how to control systems more intelligent than ourselves'. Covers the US-China rivalry.

works.author: liz-shuler
works.title: AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler's Speech to the National Press Club
works.channel: AFL-CIO speeches (National Press Club Headliners, Workers Memorial Day)
works.note: Prepared remarks, about 3,000 words. Calls AI 'the single biggest threat to working people of our lifetime, if we don't harness it properly'. Uses an Amazon 'time off task' death case to argue algorithmic management and surveillance are a worker-safety issue. Says labor is 'not anti-technology... anti-greed'. Calls for guardrails on AI in hiring, firing and pay, ties AI to the 2026 midterms, and wants worker voice at the design table. Original aflcio.org URL returns 403 to plain GET; this is an Internet Archive snapshot.

works.author: liz-shuler
works.title: Shuler's Speech at AFL-CIO and Microsoft's New Tech-Labor Partnership Event
works.note: About 1,000 words. Announces the AFL-CIO and Microsoft labor-neutrality and AI partnership. Says AI right now is 'the Wild West' and that 70% of workers fear replacement. Recalls the Senate AI Insight Forum, where she says even Zuckerberg, Gates and Altman agreed on guardrails. Casts unions as 'a stabilizing force' and a counterweight, using the IBEW electrification analogy. A cooperative, partnership-minded stance in contrast to her 2026 speech. Brad Smith speaks after her but is not on this page. Internet Archive snapshot, since the original returns 403.

works.author: liz-shuler
works.title: Pres. Shuler's Speech at 2024 Labor Innovation and Technology Summit
works.channel: AFL-CIO speeches (SAG-AFTRA/AFL-CIO Labor Innovation & Technology Summit, Las Vegas, during CES)
works.note: About 800 words. Argues that worker fear of AI destabilizes the economy and politics and that unions are the needed counterweight. Calls for a 'massive campaign to educate the public on A.I.'. Cites UNITE HERE's anti-automation win, the SAG-AFTRA and WGA AI terms, and the Microsoft deal, and criticizes 'overreach by companies... at CES'. Exact day is approximate (summit held in the CES week of January 2024; page lists related items dated 2024-01-09). Partly overlaps the December 2023 Microsoft speech. Internet Archive snapshot.

works.author: sean-o-brien
works.title: Big Beautiful Bill could give free pass to Big Tech to kill jobs
works.note: About 550 words, bylined by O'Brien. Opposes the 10-year federal moratorium on state AI regulation in the reconciliation bill and calls it Big Tech lobbying. Says AI is already displacing blue- and white-collar workers and enabling deepfakes, voice cloning and fraud. Defends state rules on AI surveillance, driverless vehicles and workplace automation. Populist, federalist framing aimed at a conservative audience.

works.author: sean-o-brien
works.title: Shifting Gears: Issues Impacting the Trucking and Commercial Bus Industries in the U.S. (testimony and prepared statement of Sean M. O'Brien)
works.channel: US Senate Commerce Committee, Surface Transportation subcommittee (Senate Hearing 119-173, GovInfo)
works.note: Full hearing record. O'Brien's prepared statement (several thousand words) has an 'Autonomous Vehicles' section. It calls unregulated AVs 'unequivocally a threat to safety... and the existence of good jobs' and asks for a federal AV framework in the surface reauthorization that does not preempt states. It praises senators for striking the state-AI-law moratorium. In the speaker-labelled Q&A he says 'Our biggest fight... is automation' and discusses port automation and the levels of automation. The record also contains other witnesses (e.g. Fred Ferguson of the American Bus Association) and topics such as tariffs, Amazon and English proficiency; extract only O'Brien's labelled sections.

works.author: duncan-crabtree-ireland
works.title: Creative Economy and Generative AI: FTC roundtable transcript
works.note: Speaker-labelled transcript, 40 pages; his own turns are about 580 words. Says generative AI 'poses a threat to the livelihoods of many' but SAG-AFTRA is 'not opposed to... the use of AI'. Wants AI to augment, not replace, human creativity. Stresses consent, compensation and IP rights over digital replicas, and notes accessibility benefits for disabled performers. Other speakers include Lina Khan and creative-sector workers; extract only his labelled turns. WebFetch loaded the PDF, but a curl GET from this machine got 404/403 (bot filtering), so recheck it in the fetch pipeline.

works.author: erik-brynjolfsson
works.title: The Turing Trap: The Promise & Peril of Human-Like Artificial Intelligence
works.note: Sole author, about 6,000 words. Argues that pursuing human-like AI (automation) erodes workers' bargaining power and concentrates wealth and power, while augmentation creates more value and shares it. Says tax policy, executive incentives and technologists' goals all tilt toward automation, and proposes rebalancing them. The amacad.org Daedalus page returns 403 to plain GET, so the arXiv PDF is used. Date is the arXiv posting (January 2022).

works.author: erik-brynjolfsson
works.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence
works.channel: Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper
works.note: Co-authored with Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen; Brynjolfsson is lead author. Uses ADP payroll data: no economy-wide displacement, but employment of 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs has fallen sharply. Losses are concentrated where AI automates rather than augments. Empirical paper with policy implications rather than an essay. The November 2025 revision is the one linked from his homepage; the original August 2025 path now serves an August 2026 update. Day of month approximate.

works.author: erik-brynjolfsson
works.title: Generative AI at Work
works.channel: NBER Working Paper 31161 (later Quarterly Journal of Economics)
works.note: Co-authored with Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond. Field study of an AI assistant for 5,000+ customer-support agents. Productivity rose about 14% on average, gains were largest for novice and low-skill workers, and AI diffused top workers' tacit knowledge. Evidence for AI as a skill-compressing complement. The PDF is the November 2023 revision; date is the original April 2023 release, day approximate.

works.author: erik-brynjolfsson
works.title: Machines of mind: The case for an AI-powered productivity boom
works.note: Co-authored with Martin Neil Baily and Anton Korinek. Argues generative AI could lift productivity growth substantially by speeding up cognitive work and innovation itself. Flags distributional risks, labor displacement and the need for policy to share gains. A techno-optimist macro counterweight to Acemoglu's pessimism already on the map.

works.author: david-autor
works.title: AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class
works.note: Sole author, about 6,000 words. Argues that AI, unlike past computerization, can let workers without elite credentials do expert decision-making in medicine, law, trades and so on, restoring middle-skill work. Says this is a possibility, not a forecast, and depends on design and policy choices. Rejects 'AI will take all jobs' fatalism. Same text as NBER w32140 'Applying AI to Rebuild Middle Class Jobs', so don't add both.

works.author: david-autor
works.title: A Better Way to Think About AI
works.channel: The Atlantic (author-posted PDF on MIT Economics site)
works.note: Co-authored with James Manyika (Google SVP), about 3,500 words. Argues that the fixation on automation is a choice and that AI should be built as a collaborator that enhances human expertise. Distinguishes automation from collaboration tools and discusses who decides the direction. The original Atlantic URL is paywalled, so this links the MIT-hosted copy. Co-author's Google role is a tech-industry tie worth noting.

works.author: david-autor
works.title: Review of Maximilian Kasy, 'The Means of Prediction: How AI Really Works (and Who Benefits)'
works.note: Sole author, about 1,300 words. Endorses reframing AI as political economy: the conflicts are 'among' people over control of data, compute and decision rights, not humans against machines. Uses an enclosure analogy for training on creators' work, which brings productivity gains but 'baleful' distribution and no democratic process. Short but dense with positions. Month from the filename; day approximate.

works.author: david-autor
works.title: The Labor Market Impacts of Technological Change: From Unbridled Enthusiasm to Qualified Optimism to Vast Uncertainty
works.channel: NBER Working Paper 30074 (prepared for Brookings Global Forum on Democracy and Technology)
works.note: Sole author, about 12,000 words. Intellectual history of how economists have thought about technology and work: from skill-biased enthusiasm, to task-based polarization, to deep uncertainty about AI. Argues that technology's labor effects are shaped by institutions and choices, not destiny. Pre-ChatGPT but sets out his long-established view. Revised July 2022.

works.author: david-autor
works.title: Beyond Job Displacement: How AI Could Reshape the Value of Human Expertise
works.channel: Digitalist Papers (author-posted PDF on MIT Economics site)
works.note: Co-authored with Neil Thompson (MIT), about 9,000 words. Sets out an 'expertise framework': transformative AI will reshape the value of expertise rather than simply remove jobs. Runs scenarios from gradual automation to full human-labor obsolescence and discusses how to prepare. The PDF has minor encoding errors but its text extracts cleanly. Date approximate (2025 Digitalist volume); confirm.

works.author: joy-buolamwini
works.title: Written Testimony, Hearing on Facial Recognition Technology (Part 1): Its Impact on our Civil Rights and Liberties
works.channel: US House Committee on Oversight and Reform
works.note: About 7,000 words, 20-page PDF (text extracted fine). Sets out her bias audits of IBM, Microsoft and Amazon, the limits of facial analysis, and calls for a moratorium on law-enforcement use, plus disclosure and accountability rules.

works.author: joy-buolamwini
works.title: Artificial Intelligence Has a Problem With Gender and Racial Bias. Here's How to Solve It
works.note: About 750 words. Machines are not neutral; error rates up to 35% for darker-skinned women; homogeneous teams and data; a moratorium on police facial recognition; the Safe Face Pledge; inclusion in AI governance.

works.author: joy-buolamwini
works.title: In the Beginning: Welcome to the Poet of Code Newsletter
works.note: About 800 words, free. Her account of the White House AI roundtable with Biden: biometric rights, wrongful facial-recognition arrests, opposition to the TSA face-scan pilot and 'surveillance creep', praise for the EU AI Act ban on live public biometrics.

works.author: joy-buolamwini
works.title: Civil Rights Implications of the Federal Use of Facial Recognition Technology: Written Testimony
works.channel: US Commission on Civil Rights (hosted on ajl.org)
works.note: About 3,500 to 4,000 words. Regulate facial analysis, recognition and remote biometrics together; TSA consent failures (#InPlaneSight survey); face templates can be reverse-engineered; disaggregated error rates; even accurate systems enable surveillance; independent audits.

works.author: joy-buolamwini
works.title: Proximity to Magnificent Power
works.note: About 600 words. Reflection on meeting Pope Leo XIV before his AI encyclical: the people harmed are absent from halls of power; an AI race for supremacy could destroy livelihoods and environments; AI must respect human dignity, not just serve 'the privileged few'. Partly personal and reflective, so fewer positions than the testimonies.

works.author: safiya-noble
works.title: Social Inequality Will Not Be Solved By an App
works.note: About 1,500 words, published around her book launch (probably adapted from Algorithms of Oppression). AI and algorithms hide value choices; commercial search reinforces racism; calls for public-interest alternatives and attention to structural inequality. WebFetch is blocked for wired.com, but a plain curl GET returns the full text.

works.author: safiya-noble
works.title: The Loss of Public Goods to Big Tech
works.note: About 1,500 words. 'We will not compute our way out of these crises'; tech profits from disaster capitalism and surveillance; tax avoidance starves public institutions; platforms amplify disinformation and racism; AI moderation raises risk; calls for regulation, restoration and reparation.

works.author: safiya-noble
works.title: The complex questions that arise when algorithms and AI intersect with race (Code Switch)
works.note: Official NPR transcript with speaker labels (NOBLE: / LIZARRAGA:). Noble is the main guest. Topics: Hollywood and the tech industry shape the public imaginary of AI; AI and race; search and generative AI harms. works.author: ruha-benjamin
works.title: The New Artificial Intelligentsia
works.channel: Los Angeles Review of Books (Legacies of Eugenics series)
works.note: About 5,500 words, her strongest AI statement. AGI hype and AI doom serve the same power grab; 'AI safety' can concentrate power; TESCREAL ideologies trace back to eugenics; rejects inevitability (creative-worker lawsuits, Hollywood strikes); hidden costs (false arrests, MiDAS, ghost labour, data centres); 'ancestral intelligence'.

works.author: ruha-benjamin
works.title: Is technology our savior -- or our slayer?
works.note: Solo talk of about 1,400 words. The transcript is embedded as JSON in the static HTML that a plain GET returns. A small elite imposes futures of AI superintelligence, space travel and bunkers while treating healthcare and housing as unimaginable; tech booms deepen inequality and surveillance (Atlanta); community platforms (Barcelona's Decidim); a collective imagination of justice. The page also carries a TED-written summary block, which must be excluded.

works.author: ruha-benjamin
works.title: Imagining 2025 and Beyond with Dr. Ruha Benjamin
works.note: Lightly edited transcript with speaker labels ('Dr. Ruha Benjamin:' / 'Justin Hendrix:'); about 5,000 words from her. Innovation versus equity; biased training records; border-tech surveillance; Sidewalk Labs as 'democratic theater'; criticism of quasi-religious AI hype and doom; data workers leading change.

works.author: kate-crawford
works.title: Generative AI's environmental costs are soaring -- and mostly secret
works.note: About 900 words, free. Energy (a generative search uses 4 to 5 times a normal search; AI could need as much energy as nations), freshwater cooling, corporate secrecy about footprints; backs the AI Environmental Impacts Act as a start and calls for mandatory disclosure. Competing interest: employed by Microsoft Research. WebFetch hits a cookie redirect, but curl -L returns the full text.

works.author: kate-crawford
works.title: Eating the Future: The Metabolic Logic of AI Slop
works.note: About 2,200 words plus notes. AI slop is structural to computational capitalism; 'metabolic images'; a metabolic rift (Marx and Foster) in ecology and information; extraction of energy, water and minerals with Global South costs; model collapse; engagement economics of slop; 'post-synthetic' alternatives. The exact day is not shown (published September 2025).

works.author: kate-crawford
works.title: The Anxieties of Big Data
works.note: About 1,800 words. An older precursor on big data and surveillance, not AI as such: GCHQ/NSA mass collection, 'surveillant anxiety', the myth that more data yields truth. Use with caution; the publication day is approximate (May 2014). Her NYT 2016 and Nature 2019/2021 AI pieces are paywalled, Excavating AI is co-authored with Trevor Paglen, and the Guardian interview blocks plain GETs.

works.author: rumman-chowdhury
works.title: Submitted Written Testimony, Artificial Intelligence: Advancing Innovation Towards the National Interest
works.channel: US House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology
works.note: 5-page PDF, about 2,100 words. 'AI is not inherently neutral, trustworthy, nor beneficial'; 'governance is innovation' (brakes let you drive faster); model access for independent audits; legal protection for red-teaming and ethical hacking; a non-regulatory technology body; join global oversight. The PDF header says 'JULY 22, 2023', a typo for the June 22 hearing.

works.author: rumman-chowdhury
works.title: AI Desperately Needs Global Oversight
works.note: About 1,400 words. Scraped public data trains generative AI that threatens jobs; models built on a public resource should be accountable; proposes an independent global governance board with access, red-teaming and enforcement powers. WebFetch is blocked for wired.com, but a plain curl GET returns the full text.

works.author: rumman-chowdhury
works.title: What the Global AI Governance Conversation Misses
works.note: About 1,000 words, readable without login. Global Majority countries (for example the Pacific) face AI risks as they come online; expanding access needs matching investment in safeguards and evaluation; proposes regional AI safety institutes. Written while she was US Science Envoy for AI.

works.author: rumman-chowdhury
works.title: 'AI for Good' shouldn't become the new innovation arbitrage
works.note: About 1,000 words, written after the Paris AI Action Summit. 'AI for Good' can turn low-resource communities into testbeds for unproven tech (the $100 laptop analogy); calls for safeguards, community engagement and evaluation. A 2026 Tech Policy Press piece on AI agents was excluded because it is co-authored with Konstantinos Komaitis.

works.author: cory-doctorow
works.title: The AI hype bubble is the new crypto hype bubble
works.note: About 2,500 words in the lead essay; the daily post also has a link roundup, which must be excluded. LLMs as autocomplete; incumbents drive the hype; 'criti-hype' (x-risk talk distracts from corporate power; corporations as 'slow AIs'); the real threat to creative workers is wage cuts; keep machine output uncopyrightable; collective, non-assignable artist rights.

works.author: cory-doctorow
works.title: What kind of bubble is AI?
works.note: About 1,800 words. AI is a bubble; bubbles differ by what they leave behind; inference costs are subsidized; high-value uses need near-perfect reliability, so the business case rests on replacing workers; 'reverse centaurs'; policy ignores the systemic risk of dependence on AI that may vanish.

works.author: cory-doctorow
works.title: The real (economic) AI apocalypse is nigh
works.note: About 1,900 words. A monopolist-driven bubble; 'dogshit unit economics'; circular Microsoft/OpenAI/Nvidia deals and GPU-collateralized debt; a crash is near-inevitable; puncture it early and prepare to absorb the residue (cheap compute, open models, talent); AI as a 'normal technology'; the danger is financial mania, not superintelligence.

works.author: cory-doctorow
works.title: The Reverse-Centaur's Guide to Criticizing AI
works.channel: Pluralistic (text of a University of Washington lecture)
works.note: About 6,000 words, adapted from his 2026 book manuscript; his most complete statement. Hype serves growth-stock monopolies; reverse centaurs and 'accountability sinks'; automation blindness; AI art lacks communicative intent; opposes new training-copyright rules; keep AI output in the public domain; sectoral bargaining; dismisses doom scenarios.

works.author: cory-doctorow
works.title: The AI bubble isn't like the internet bubble
works.note: About 1,500 words. Workers smuggled in the early web bottom-up, but bosses mandate and monitor AI use top-down; web unit economics improved with scale while AI's worsen; worker autonomy decides whether AI makes centaurs or reverse centaurs.

works.author: russell-moore
works.title: AI Might Teach, But It Can't Preach
works.note: About 1,200 words. Argues AI may research, write and even deliver sermons, but preaching is a personal word from a fellow redeemed sinner known to the congregation; criticises undisclosed AI-written sermons.

works.author: russell-moore
works.title: A New Era of AI Is Here, and the Church Is Not Ready
works.note: About 1,300 words. Compares AI to the printing press and television; warns people confide spiritual questions to chatbots and get wrong answers; uses the 'Father Justin' bot as a cautionary case; says hyper-personalisation serves marketing, not persons. Membership prompts on the page but the full text loads.

works.author: russell-moore
works.title: A Different Image of God for an Era of AI
works.note: About 1,000 words. Argues the church is unprepared because it defines the imago Dei by functions (reason, relationship) that machines can imitate; says the image of God is a 'who' (Jesus), not a 'what'; sceptical of transhumanist mind-uploading. The page shows no exact day; the date is the issue month.

works.author: russell-moore
works.title: Chatbot Companionship Will Make Our Loneliness Crisis Worse
works.note: About 1,000 words. Argues AI companions offer 'relationship without tension' and deepen isolation; criticises the profit motives and techno-optimism of Andreessen, Zuckerberg and Musk; singles out erotic AI; calls the church to offer real community.

works.author: russell-moore
works.title: AI Is OK (Sort Of)
works.note: About 500 words. Older, from his ERLC period around the 2019 evangelical AI statement (that statement is co-signed and is not included here). Says AI cannot disciple anyone but can speed Bible translation; says stopping AI is unrealistic, so discern dangers early. Useful as a baseline for how his view has changed. The https URL redirects to http.

works.author: reid-hoffman
works.title: OpenAI and AI Futures
works.note: About 900 words. Older baseline: backs nonprofit labs as a counterweight to commercial competition; calls for 'open benefit to humanity' rather than open source for its own sake; calls for broad public and policymaker conversation. Commercial interest: he was then an OpenAI funder and later a board member. The article loads without login (overlays only).

works.author: reid-hoffman
works.title: Superagency
works.note: About 1,050 words, his own short statement of the Superagency thesis (the book itself is co-written with Greg Beato; this post has his name only). Admits risks to agency, jobs, privacy, misinformation and corporate dominance, then argues AI as a 'super-tool' expands agency even for non-users. Commercial interests: Greylock partner, Inflection AI and Manas AI co-founder, Microsoft board member.

works.author: reid-hoffman
works.title: AI, Society, and Our World Order
works.channel: reidhoffman.org (lecture at the London School of Economics)
works.note: About 4,000 to 4,500 words, the richest single source. AI is 'value-sculpted', not neutral; defends iterative deployment; says measure risk before regulating and do not pause; acknowledges real Luddite-style disruption; frames AI as a geopolitical amplifier and argues for speed and Global South inclusion. Minor transcription typos. Commercial interests as above.

works.author: reid-hoffman
works.title: No, AI isn't coming to destroy us. But it will transform the world
works.note: About 950 words. Rejects the doom framing; sets aside the question of when AGI arrives and predicts AI will be far more capable and woven into daily life within three years, so that by 2028 going without it will feel unthinkable. The page metadata marks it as not free, but the full text loaded.

works.author: reid-hoffman
works.title: Move fast and make things: the new career mantra
works.note: About 985 words, on AI and jobs for graduates. Concedes near-term job cuts, especially entry-level; advises people to 'AI-optimise' their careers rather than AI-proof them; says intention, emotional intelligence and networks matter more. The page metadata marks it as not free, but the full text loaded.

works.author: fei-fei-li
works.title: Governing AI Through Acquisition and Procurement (testimony to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee)
works.channel: U.S. Senate HSGAC, hosted by Stanford HAI
works.note: About 2,300 words of written testimony (PDF; text checked with pdftotext). Wants to demystify 'wild claims' from both hype and doom; AI benefits for healthcare and caregiving; privacy and fairness safeguards; transparent government procurement; strong public AI research investment. Given in her individual capacity.

works.author: fei-fei-li
works.title: 'The Godmother of AI' says California's well-intended AI bill will harm the U.S. ecosystem
works.note: About 620 words. Opposes SB 1047: developer liability for misuse, kill-switch harms to open source, damage to academic research, an arbitrary compute threshold, and no attention to present harms like bias and deepfakes; still backs governance and offers to work with Sen. Wiener. Written shortly after she launched the startup World Labs.

works.author: fei-fei-li
works.title: Briefing to the UN Security Council on AI and international peace and security (9821st meeting)

Calls for a public-sector 'moonshot', a multilateral AI research institute, closing digital divides, evidence-based governance and human dignity.

works.author: fei-fei-li
works.title: From Words to Worlds: Spatial Intelligence is AI's Next Frontier
works.note: About 3,500 words, mostly technical (world models), with clear societal positions: AI should augment rather than replace people; rejects both utopian and apocalyptic narratives; respect for human dignity and agency in caregiving and robotics.
