works.title: Peter Thiel on Political Correctness, Stagnation and Inequality (Conversations with Tyler, Ep. 1)
works.note: Speaker-labelled (TYLER COWEN / PETER THIEL). States the 'atoms vs bits' stagnation thesis, says AI is 'slightly overhyped', argues the story of mass job replacement by computers is probably wrong, blames regulation and technocratic agencies for slow progress, and calls the US a representative republic run by unelected agencies rather than a democracy. Long, about 10k words. Older, but the stagnation view it sets out is long established.

works.author: peter-thiel
works.title: COSM talk: The Failures and 'Self-Hatred' of Big Tech (Mind Matters Ep. 156 transcript)
works.channel: Mind Matters podcast (Discovery Institute), talk given at COSM 2019
works.note: PDF transcript with speaker labels (Peter Thiel / George Gilder). Sets out his 'crypto is libertarian, AI is communist' argument: AI as a centralising, surveillance technology that the Chinese state loves. Also argues big tech is quasi-communist and that the computer age has failed to deliver. About 5.5k words. Thiel's talk is most of it; Gilder only introduces him. The talk dates from COSM 2019; 2021-10-21 is a placeholder, so check the podcast release date.

works.author: peter-thiel
works.title: Thiel on AI & Racing with China (transcribed excerpt of Joe Rogan Experience, Aug 2024)
works.channel: LessWrong (excerpt posted by Ben Pace) of the Joe Rogan Experience
works.note: Speaker-labelled (Thiel / Rogan) partial transcript of the AI section of a podcast published 2024-08-16. Thiel: global compute governance 'sounds even worse'; a military AI race with China makes AI more dangerous; the CCP might restrain AI to protect its own control; doomer and EA narratives are 'winning the arguments'; there is no good endgame for drone autonomy. Caveat: abridged, with commentary by the poster. Use only the lines labelled Thiel.

works.author: andrej-karpathy
works.title: Auto-grading decade-old Hacker News discussions with hindsight
works.note: Own blog. Argues that LLM judgment can audit past public speech at scale, that 'security by obscurity' for online behaviour ends once intelligence is 'too cheap to meter' (his advice is 'best to be good'), and that future-prediction models are desirable. Bears on surveillance and accountability. Medium length.

works.author: andrej-karpathy
works.title: Vibe coding MenuGen
works.note: Own blog. Argues AI is lowering the barrier to building software toward zero ('as easy as making a TikTok'), but says vibe-coding full apps is not yet fit for anything important, and questions forecasts that society will be automated by 2027 because so much work is hidden in GUIs LLMs can't reach. Positions on work, who can build, and automation timelines. About 2.5k words.

works.author: mark-zuckerberg
works.title: Mark Zuckerberg's Remarks at AI Forum
works.channel: Meta Newsroom (remarks as prepared, US Senate AI Insight Forum)
works.note: Prepared remarks to the Schumer AI Insight Forum. Names safety and access as the two defining issues. Says government is ultimately responsible for balancing innovation and safeguards and that Congress should engage. Makes a qualified case for open source (more secure, levels the playing field, lets the US rather than others set the global standard) and says Meta would reconsider if systems approached superintelligence. Short, about 1k words.

works.author: mark-zuckerberg
works.title: Transcript for Mark Zuckerberg: First Interview in the Metaverse (Lex Fridman Podcast #398)
works.note: Speaker-labelled. Zuckerberg says opening Llama 2 had value 'significantly greater than the risks'. He opposes a single dominant AI in favour of many AIs that empower many people, describes safety review before release, and discusses AI personas and creator AIs. Much of the episode is about the metaverse and codec avatars, so the AI-society content is partial.

works.author: mark-zuckerberg
works.title: Meta (META) Q4 2025 Earnings Call Transcript
works.channel: Meta earnings call (transcript via The Motley Fool)
works.note: Speaker-labelled ('Mark Elliot Zuckerberg:'), about 2.4k words of his remarks. Says 2026 is the year AI 'starts to dramatically change the way that we work'. Describes flattening teams, with one talented person now doing what big teams did. Restates the 'personal superintelligence' vision built on personal context, and suggests frontier AI may not always be offered through an API to everyone. Caveat: corporate and investor framing; AI-assisted transcript that may contain errors.

works.author: yann-lecun
works.title: Open Hearing: Advancing Intelligence in the Era of Artificial Intelligence (S. Hrg. 118-118), statement and testimony of Yann LeCun
works.channel: US Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (GPO record)
works.note: Official GPO hearing record, speaker-labelled ('Dr. LeCun.'), with his full opening statement and Q&A. He argues AI is a foundational open platform and that open-sourcing base models democratises access and strengthens US and democratic leadership. He supports common standards among democracies, transparency and red-teaming, calls the White House voluntary commitments 'a critical step', says text watermarking is hard and posters should be responsible, and says current AI is far from human-level. Other witnesses (Jensen, Ding) also appear. The committee's own PDF of the statement blocks bots (403), so use this govinfo copy.

works.author: demis-hassabis
works.title: Transcript from an interview with Demis Hassabis (Nobel Week)
works.note: Q&A format with answers labelled 'Demis Hassabis:', about 4.5k words. Says how AI's benefits are shared is a geopolitical question that society must decide collectively. Names two concerns: bad actors repurposing general-purpose AI, and keeping control of increasingly autonomous, agent-like systems. Also covers open science and diversity in research. Caveat: WebFetch got 403 from nobelprize.org, but a plain curl GET returns the full text (HTTP 200).

works.author: demis-hassabis
works.title: Introducing Gemini: our largest and most capable AI model
works.note: Bylined 'By Demis Hassabis ... on behalf of the Gemini team'; it opens with a separate note from Sundar Pichai, which should be excluded. Hassabis frames AI as his life's work toward general, helpful AI and has a responsibility-and-safety section on evaluations, red-teaming and working with outside experts. Mostly a product announcement, so it is thin on positions about society. Lower priority.

works.author: leopold-aschenbrenner
works.title: II. From AGI to Superintelligence: the Intelligence Explosion
works.note: About 6k words. Argues that automated AI research could compress a decade of progress into about a year, that the period after would be 'one of the most volatile, tense, dangerous' in history with a real risk of losing control, and that superintelligence would give decisive military and economic advantage. Fills the missing chapter between I and IIIa.

works.author: leopold-aschenbrenner
works.title: IIIa. Racing to the Trillion-Dollar Cluster
works.note: About 4-5k words. Says AGI datacenters must be built in America or close democratic allies, not autocracies such as Gulf states. Calls for natural-gas power and sweeping permitting and utility deregulation, and argues that automating white-collar wages (tens of trillions of dollars a year) justifies trillion-dollar investment. Positions on power, industrial policy and jobs.

works.author: leopold-aschenbrenner
works.title: V. Parting Thoughts
works.note: Short. Rejects both doomers (pause proposals naive, underrate authoritarian misuse) and e/acc (shallow, deny real AGI, take authoritarian money), and sets out 'AGI Realism': superintelligence is a national-security matter, America must lead, and the risks must be managed seriously. Useful as a direct statement of where he sits between the two camps.

works.author: leopold-aschenbrenner
works.title: Nobody's on the ball on AGI alignment
works.note: Own blog, about 16 minutes' reading. Argues alignment research is vastly under-resourced (about 300 researchers against about 100k on capabilities) and that RLHF will fail on superhuman models. Calls for an Apollo or Warp Speed scale effort, puts AI existential risk at about 5% over 20 years, and predicts a strong public reaction to AI like the early COVID shift. Shows his views before Situational Awareness, a different occasion.

works.author: alex-karp
works.title: Palantir (PLTR) Q3 2025 Earnings Call Transcript
works.channel: Palantir earnings call (transcript via The Motley Fool)
works.note: Speaker-labelled ('Alexander C. Karp:'), about 1.1k words of his remarks. Argues AI rewards workers with hands-on domain skill (factory staff, truck drivers) over credentialed generalists, who face 'destructive' pressure. Says American workers should get rich from AI, that AI gives America 'a massive unfair advantage' over a 'stagnant Europe', and frames the company as meritocratic and anti-woke. Caveats: promotional, AI-assisted transcript, and some lines mislabelled (the border remarks are Shyam Sankar's). Proposed as a replacement because Palantir's own letter pages render only through JavaScript (see final report).

works.author: alex-karp
works.title: Palantir (PLTR) Q4 2025 Earnings Call Transcript
works.channel: Palantir earnings call (transcript via The Motley Fool)
works.note: Speaker-labelled, about 2-2.5k words of his remarks across six turns. Says AI's new 'haves' are workers who can use the software, not only capital owners, which he says confounds political leaders. Says value sits in orchestration and the ontology, not commodity LLMs. Criticises European and Canadian procurement, warns that political pressure could push those countries toward extremes, and casts Palantir as defending 'the noble side of the West' within US law. Caveats: promotional, and some garbled passages.

works.author: elon-musk
works.title: Tesla (TSLA) Q3 2025 Earnings Call Transcript
works.channel: Tesla earnings call (transcript via The Motley Fool)
works.note: Speaker-labelled, about 4k words of Musk. Says he wants enough voting control for 'strong influence' over a future 'robot army' and is not comfortable building it otherwise. Claims humanoid robots will be about 5x as productive as people and could make work optional, frames the mission as 'sustainable abundance' and the end of poverty, and calls proxy advisers 'corporate terrorists'. Positions on power, concentration and jobs. Caveat: investor framing.

works.author: helen-toner
works.title: 2 big questions for AI progress in 2025-2026
works.note: About 4,000 words, sole author. Asks whether AI will get good at tasks beyond math and coding, which are hard to verify, and what that means for timelines and for policy.

works.author: helen-toner
works.title: Testimony before the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, IP, AI and the Internet: 'Protecting Our Edge: Trade Secrets and the Global AI Arms Race'
works.channel: U.S. House Judiciary Committee (hosted by CSET)
works.note: Written testimony, about 3,000 words. Covers US-China competition in frontier AI, protecting trade secrets and company cybersecurity, transparency, and whistleblower protections for AI employees. Discloses her OpenAI board service (2021-23). Replaces the Senate Judiciary PDF, which returns 403 to a plain GET.

works.author: helen-toner
works.title: Testimony before the U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary: 'Stealth Stealing: China's Ongoing Theft of U.S. Innovation'
works.channel: U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee (hosted by CSET)
works.note: Written testimony, about 4,300 words. Argues Chinese labs use distillation on US models, backs light-touch frontier transparency and disclosure requirements, supports strengthening NIST's work, and calls for employees to be able to raise concerns. Caveat: a footnote says it is adapted from earlier testimony, so some text overlaps the 2025 House testimony.

works.author: alondra-nelson
works.title: Remarks of Dr. Alondra Nelson at the White House Gathering on Technology, Civil Rights, and Democratic Values
works.note: Prepared remarks, about 1,600 words, given at the launch of the AI Bill of Rights Blueprint. Sets out its five protections (safe and effective systems, protection from algorithmic discrimination, data privacy, notice and explanation, human alternatives). Ties technology to civil rights and democracy. A speaker-labelled own-voice replacement for the unlabelled Edge Dialogues transcript. Caveat: she gave it as a government official.

works.author: alondra-nelson
works.title: Remarks of Dr. Alondra Nelson at the Launch of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
works.note: Prepared remarks, about 1,900 words. Argues for building rights and risk management into AI from the start, says government must act now on AI harms (kids, civil rights, hate and harassment), and treats the framework as a step toward accountability. Caveat: she gave it as a government official.

works.author: anton-korinek
works.title: Preparing the Workforce for an Uncertain AI Future (Written Statement to the U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum on Workforce)
works.channel: U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum (hosted by Brookings)
works.note: Written statement, sole author, 5 pages. Argues we are entering an era of cognitive automation, that shared prosperity needs policy (steering AI progress and updating how institutions distribute income), and that scenario planning should include AI automating most work within 5-20 years. Ends with two recommendations to the Senate. Replaces the unlabelled FLI and CAIP podcast transcripts.

works.author: anton-korinek
works.title: AI's Economic Peril
works.channel: Journal of Democracy 34(4) (author manuscript linked from korinek.com)
works.note: About 4,300 words. Co-author: Stephanie A. Bell (Partnership on AI), equal billing. Argues that AI-driven labour displacement and concentrated gains threaten democracy, and calls for steering AI toward worker-complementing uses and for income support. The journal's own page shows only an excerpt; this full manuscript is hosted on Dropbox and returns with dl=1.

works.author: anton-korinek
works.title: The future of tax policy: A public finance framework for the age of AI
works.note: About 2,500 words. Co-author: Lee M. Lockwood. Argues that AI erodes the labour tax base, and that tax policy must shift toward capital, consumption and AI rents to fund public goods and income support. Conflict: the editor's note says Korinek holds an unpaid seat on Anthropic's Economic Advisory Council; the owner should review.

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Written Testimony, Hearing on 'The Philosophy of AI: Learning from History, Shaping Our Future'
works.channel: U.S. Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee (hosted by MIT Shaping the Future of Work)
works.note: Sole author, about 6,500 words. Names three risks: inequality-driven social tension, AI's control over information and manipulation (a threat to democracy), and shifts in norms. Argues the direction of technology is a choice and calls for policy to redirect AI away from automation and surveillance. Replaces the unlabelled Jon Stewart and MoneyWeek interview transcripts.

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Written Comments for AI Workforce Forum
works.channel: U.S. Senate AI Insight Forum (hosted by MIT Shaping the Future of Work)
works.note: Sole author, about 2,000 words. Argues that generative AI could be pro-worker, but we are heading toward automation and surveillance that raise inequality and limit wage growth. Warns that monopolized AI widens the gap between capital and labour. Proposes policy levers, including government-set goals for pro-worker AI and a more even tax treatment of hiring labour versus investing in automation (cutting payroll taxes, reducing capital deductions).

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Nobel Lecture: Institutions, Technology, and Prosperity
works.note: Sole author, about 21,000 words (a long academic text). Links inclusive institutions to the direction of technology. Later sections apply this to AI: automation versus new tasks, concentrated power, and the need for institutions to steer AI. It acknowledges joint work with Robinson and Johnson, but he wrote it alone. The AI sections are the relevant part.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: On AI and Children
works.note: About 3,000 words, sole author. Sets out conjectures on child safety: pushes back on claims like 'AI is harmful for children', says liability and lawsuits are already producing age detection, parental controls and guardrails, and is wary of the flood of state child-safety bills.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: "These Parchment Barriers"
works.channel: Hyperdimensional (Substack); reproduces the OpenAI AI Futures blog launch post
works.note: About 1,800 words, his own launch post. On concentration of power: no one company or oligopoly should control the economy or the architecture of society, humans should keep autonomy and the right to use AI anonymously, and decentralization alone is not enough. Flag: Ball now leads OpenAI's Strategic Futures team. He says the views are his own, but the piece is also on OpenAI's site, so the owner should review.

works.author: samuel-hammond
works.title: AI and Leviathan: Part III
works.note: About 3,500 words, sole author. Completes the series already on the map (Parts I-II). Argues that AI will upend institutions as the printing press did by changing transaction costs. Liberal democracy must stay in Acemoglu-Robinson's 'narrow corridor' between a stronger state and a stronger society.

works.author: samuel-hammond
works.title: Why AGI is closer than you think
works.note: About 4,500 words, sole author. Makes the case for short AGI timelines, the premise behind his institutional-disruption arguments. It states a clear position on AI timelines but says less on social policy.

works.author: samuel-hammond
works.title: The Sorcerer's Apprentice
works.note: About 2,000 words, sole author. Responds to the 2026 OpenAI sandbox-escape disclosure. Argues that open-ended reinforcement learning will give superhuman agents across domains, that alignment is falling behind, and that the labs should have known better.

works.author: noah-smith
works.title: AI keeps stubbornly refusing to take our jobs
works.note: About 2,200 words, sole author. Challenges the Silicon Valley belief that AI's main economic effect is displacing workers, using labour-market evidence that human work is holding up.

works.author: noah-smith
works.title: If AI is a weapon, why don't we regulate it like one?
works.note: About 3,700 words, sole author. On the Anthropic vs Department of War dispute. Argues the nation-state must keep a monopoly on force, so frontier AI should be regulated like weapons rather than governed by corporate contract terms. Quotes Dean Ball at length; Smith's own argument is the bulk.

works.author: noah-smith
works.title: Updated thoughts on AI risk
works.note: About 3,000 words, sole author. Explains why he moved from 'LLMs won't destroy humanity' (2023) to expecting human disempowerment, and which risks he now ranks highest. Recommends building defensive technology. A useful record of a position change.

works.author: venkatesh-rao
works.title: Our Eukaryotic Moment
works.note: About 5,000 words, sole author. Argues that the 'very powerful computer or synthetic mind' picture of AI is a misleading Ptolemaic frame. AI is better seen as a symbiotic change in the architecture of humans and institutions, and the individual human may not be the 'cell boundary'. It is a long metaphor, offered openly as speculation rather than prediction.

works.author: venkatesh-rao
works.title: Cognitive Farmsteading
works.note: About 5,300 words, sole author. Describes and recommends AI-assisted 'smallholder' intellectual culture: AI moves intellectual life from urban to rural-style, decentralized self-sufficiency. A positive, humanist-pluralist view of AI and work.

works.author: divya-siddarth
works.title: We should all get to decide what to do about AI
works.note: About 900 words, sole author. Argues that the default path (technologists build, investors direct, regulators restrain) fails for society-scale technology like AI. The public must have a direct say in AI's direction through collective-intelligence processes.

works.author: divya-siddarth
works.title: Co-owning the Future with Data Cooperatives @ Stanford HAI
works.channel: Collective Intelligence Project blog (talk at Stanford HAI Fall Conference)
works.note: A lightly edited transcript of her own talk, single speaker, about 3,000 words. Critiques 'data is the new oil' and proposes data cooperatives so the public shares ownership of, and power over, the value AI draws from data.

works.author: divya-siddarth
works.title: The Case for Collective Intelligence @ iWORD 2022
works.channel: Collective Intelligence Project blog (talk at iWORD 2022, Reimagining Democracy)
works.note: A lightly edited transcript of her own talk, single speaker, about 2,000 words. Presents collective intelligence as the way to govern transformative AI, says AI governance raises the same problems of power and scale as governance in general, and argues democracy is more than preference aggregation.

works.author: paul-kingsnorth
works.title: The Anti-Christ now rules us all
works.note: About 2,500 words, by Kingsnorth (a shorter version of his Substack essay 'What Progress Wants', so do not add both). Argues 'Progress' or the 'technium' is an inhuman spiritual force whose end is replacing humans. On the right lips, 'AI' can sound like another word for 'Anti-Christ'. Ends by asking whether we will let technology replace us. It speaks to AI less directly than his newer pieces.
